figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of OpenJarvis. (Left) Five composable primitives (Intelligence, Engine, Agents, Tools & Memory, Learning) are composed through a declarative spec that can be shared, evaluated, and optimized end-to-end (Section 3.1). (Middle) Joint accuracy-efficiency evaluation across the evaluated local specs (green) and 3 cloud baselines (blue) reveals that on-device configurations approach within 3.2 pp of the best cloud model at roughly 800$\times$ lower marginal API cost per query (Section 4.3). (Right) LLM-guided spec search uses frontier cloud models as reflective proposers: the teacher diagnoses failures, proposes edits across the full spec, and a held-out gate accepts only non-regressing improvements, closing the remaining local–cloud accuracy gap by 13–32 pp with student training on-device (Section 4.4).
figures.headline: On-device configurations approach the best cloud model within 3.2 pp at roughly 800 times lower marginal API cost per query.
citing_sentences: OpenJarvis decomposes a personal AI stack into five primitives, each with a typed interface and registry (Figure 1, left).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: OpenJarvis architecture. Five composable primitives decouple model selection (Intelligence), inference runtime (Engine), agent logic (Agents), data integration (Tools & Memory), and on-device learning (Learning) into independently swappable layers. A spec (Section 3.1) composes all five into a declarative configuration that can be shared, evaluated, and optimized end-to-end.
figures.headline: Five independently swappable layers are composed by one declarative spec that is optimized end to end.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The spec abstraction. (a) A spec is a typed configuration object with five primitives: Intelligence, Engine, Agents, Tools & Memory, and Learning. (b) Optimizers instantiate the same signature by restricting which fields they edit. LoRA edits Intelligence weights; DSPy and GEPA edit Agent prompts; LLM-guided spec search edits Intelligence, Engine, Agents, and Tools & Memory jointly.
figures.headline: A typed spec lets each optimizer edit only the fields it covers, from weight adaptation to joint edits across four primitives.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 shows the spec as a structured declaration alongside the optimization signature; Figure 9 (Appendix A.1) shows the corresponding TOML serialization.
Section 3.1 introduces the spec via the typed declaration in Figure 3.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Three ways to optimize a spec. OpenJarvis proposes edits to the four editable primitives and keeps an edit only if held-out performance does not regress. Evolutionary spec search maintains and merges a population of candidate specs [1]. Single-component baselines edit one primitive at a time.
figures.headline: Of three optimization regimes compared, only LLM-guided spec search edits all four editable primitives.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 summarizes the three regimes compared in Section 4.4: LLM-guided spec search (Algorithm 4), an evolutionary spec-search baseline (Algorithm 4), and single-component optimization (Algorithm 4); Figure 8 separates the proposer axis from the move-space axis.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Accuracy-efficiency frontier. Local configurations approach the best cloud accuracy within 3.2 pp while reducing marginal API cost by roughly 800$\times$ and end-to-end latency by roughly 4$\times$ under our benchmark protocol. Energy and hardware-specific breakdowns are in Appendix C.3.
figures.headline: Across cost and latency, every non-dominated configuration is local, while accuracy stays within 3.2 pp of the best cloud model.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 plots average accuracy against dollar cost, latency, and energy per query for the evaluated local specs and 3 cloud baselines.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: LLM-guided spec search improves local specs. Every student–teacher pair improves over the unoptimized spec on all three benchmarks. The strongest search-optimized Qwen3.5-9B student reaches 100.0% on PinchBench, 83.0% on LiveCodeBench, and 91.0% on LiveResearchBench.
figures.headline: Every student-teacher pair improves over the unoptimized spec on all three benchmarks, reaching 100.0% on PinchBench.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 shows accuracy before and after search.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Accuracy vs. optimization cost. LLM-guided spec search reaches the best accuracy on all three main benchmarks. LoRA is the strongest single-primitive baseline, but LLM-guided spec search is 7.1–10.9$\times$ cheaper to optimize. DSPy/SIMBA and prompt-only GEPA produce modest gains over the unoptimized local spec.
figures.headline: LLM-guided spec search reaches the best accuracy on all three main benchmarks at 7.1–10.9 times lower optimization cost.

Figure 7 compares LLM-guided spec search with prompt-only and weight-only baselines (DSPy/SIMBA, prompt-only GEPA, SFT, LoRA [39, 1, 31]) under the same offline protocol.

figures.caption: Proposer and move-space ablations for LLM-guided spec search. Student: Qwen3.5-9B; teacher: Claude Opus 4.6. Left: at fixed four-primitive move space, the LLM proposer outperforms a template-random proposer and evolutionary spec search. Middle: at fixed LLM proposer, expanding from one editable primitive to all four improves both accuracy and latency. Right: merging primitive pairs reduces accuracy and speedup relative to the full four-primitive spec.

Across platforms, the spec abstraction enables the same Agent and Tool configuration to be retargeted to different hardware tiers without rewriting prompts or agent logic: only the [intelligence] and [engine] slots change (Figure 9).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Edit-type allocation by benchmark. Share of accepted edits by primitive across the 8-benchmark suite. Student: Qwen3.5-9B; teacher: Claude Opus 4.6. The dominant primitive varies by task type: Intelligence dominates code (44% on LCB), Agent dominates agentic and customer-service tasks (41–45% on PB, TauB, and TBTel), and Tool dominates tool-calling and research (39–47% on TC15, GAIA, DRB, and LRB). Engine edits appear across benchmarks but primarily affect efficiency rather than standalone accuracy. Bars are normalized within benchmark.
figures.headline: The dominant primitive for accepted edits varies by task: Intelligence for code, Agents for customer-service tasks, Tools for research.
citing_sentences: The dominant primitive within that distribution tracks task structure: Intelligence edits dominate code (44% on LiveCodeBench), Agent edits dominate customer-service and agentic tasks (41–45% on PB, TauB, and TBTel), and Tool edits dominate tool-calling and research (39–47% on TC15, GAIA, DRB, and LRB; Appendix C.5, Figure 10).

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Edit-type allocation by failure cluster category. Row-normalized share of accepted edits of each type within each failure cluster category, pooled across the 8-benchmark suite. Student: Qwen3.5-9B; teacher: Claude Opus 4.6. The teacher maps diagnoses to the expected intervention type: retrieval failures receive mostly Tool edits (65%), reasoning failures mostly Intelligence edits (52%), control-flow failures mostly Agent edits (51%), efficiency-bounded failures mostly Engine edits (58%), and format/output failures mostly Agent edits (53%). This pattern supports the claim that the diagnose phase produces semantically meaningful failure clusters rather than arbitrary edit allocation.
figures.headline: Failure clusters map to matching primitives, with retrieval failures receiving mostly Tool edits at 65%.
citing_sentences: At the per-failure level, the teacher maps each diagnosis to the corresponding primitive: retrieval failures receive mostly Tool edits, reasoning failures mostly Intelligence edits, control-flow failures mostly Agent edits, and efficiency-bounded failures mostly Engine edits (Figure 11).

abstract: Personal AI stacks, like OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, are becoming central to daily work, yet they route nearly every query (often over sensitive local data) to cloud-hosted frontier models. Replacing frontier models with local models inside existing stacks does not work: swapping Claude Opus 4.6 for Qwen3.5-9B drops accuracy by 25-39 pp across personal AI tasks like PinchBench and GAIA. Existing stacks bundle agentic prompts, tool descriptions, memory configuration, and runtime settings around a specific cloud model. Only the prompts can be tuned, and state-of-the-art prompt optimizers close just 5 pp of the local-cloud gap on their own. This motivates a decomposed personal AI stack: one that exposes individual primitives which can be optimized individually or jointly to close the local-cloud gap. We present OpenJarvis, an architecture that represents a personal AI system as a typed spec over five primitives: Intelligence, Engine, Agents, Tools & Memory, and Learning. Each primitive is an independently editable field, making the stack end-to-end optimizable and measurable against accuracy, cost, and latency. Towards closing the local-cloud gap without surrendering local-model properties, OpenJarvis introduces LLM-guided spec search, a local-cloud collaboration in which frontier cloud models propose edits across the spec at search time, only non-regressing edits are accepted, and the resulting spec runs entirely on-device at inference time. With LLM-guided spec search, on-device specs match or exceed cloud accuracy on 4 of 8 benchmarks and land within 3.2 pp of the best cloud baseline on average. They also reduce marginal API cost by ~800x and end-to-end latency by 4x.

sections.body: The paper argues that personal AI stacks such as OpenClaw and Hermes Agent send queries to cloud models, and that swapping in a local model breaks them. Replacing Claude Opus 4.6 with Qwen3.5-9B, with the rest of the stack fixed, drops accuracy by 25–39 pp on PinchBench and GAIA. The authors give two causes. Substitution breaks monolithic stacks, because prompts, tool descriptions, memory and runtime settings are co-designed for the cloud model. Single-primitive optimization plateaus, because GEPA and DSPy close only 5 pp of the cloud–local gap. The authors propose OpenJarvis, a typed spec over five primitives: Intelligence, Engine, Agents, Tools & Memory and Learning, so the whole stack can be optimized end to end.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Local models lose 25–39 pp when swapped into cloud-designed personal AI stacks, and prompt tuning recovers only 5 pp.

sections.body: The related work groups prior efforts by primitive. Personal AI frameworks such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent and LangChain formalize Agents and Tools but tie Intelligence, Engine and Learning to specific cloud models. Local inference tools such as Ollama and llama.cpp cover Engine and Intelligence but provide no Agents, Tools or Learning. Optimization methods, including DSPy, GEPA and LoRA, each update one primitive at a time. Evaluation tools such as Zeus and MLCommons measure a single axis of a single primitive. The authors state that no existing framework formalizes the full five-primitive composition as one optimizable object, and they position LLM-guided spec search as complementary to single-primitive methods.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior tools each formalize part of the stack, and the authors know of no framework jointly evaluating all five primitives.

sections.body: The spec gives each of five primitives an independently editable field. LLM-guided spec search repeats four steps: diagnose failures by clustering traces, propose edits, execute candidates on a held-out gate, and commit only gated improvements. A frontier teacher proposes edits across Intelligence, Engine, Agents, and Tools & Memory, while Learning specifies how the spec is updated. An edit that targets a failure cluster is accepted only if it raises that cluster's gate score and keeps every other cluster within a tolerance of 1%. The loop stops when gate scores stagnate for five sessions. Teacher calls occur at search time only. The resulting spec runs on-device, and cloud-as-tool use is disabled in the headline configurations.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: A typed spec over five primitives lets an LLM proposer edit four of them, keeping only edits that do not regress.

sections.body: The experiments cover 8 benchmarks, 11 local models from 4 families, 3 cloud baselines and 7 hardware platforms, with results averaged over 5 independent runs. In the portability test in Table 1, substituting Qwen3.5-9B drops OpenClaw from 96.0 to 62.3 on PinchBench, and Hermes Agent from 93.5 to 68.7. An OpenJarvis spec with the same local model recovers 77% of the PinchBench drop. The best local model, Qwen3.5-122B, reaches 80.3% average accuracy against 83.5% for Claude Opus 4.6, with roughly 800$\times$ lower marginal API cost and roughly 4$\times$ lower latency. With LLM-guided spec search, Qwen3.5-9B reaches 100.0% on PinchBench, and average gains per student model range from 13.1 to 31.5 pp.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On-device specs match or exceed cloud accuracy on 4 of 8 benchmarks and land within 3.2 pp of the best cloud baseline on average.

sections.body: The authors state that frontier models are used at search time, and the resulting spec makes zero cloud calls at inference time. Undistilled local specs already match or beat cloud models on 4 of 8 benchmarks. When a frontier proposer is used, only eligible traces are transmitted. At 100 queries per day, the amortized proposer cost falls below 0.001 USD per query within six months. The authors report that the headline gains survive four perturbations: reward-weight variants, search-seed variance, random restarts and proposer comparison. Stated limitations are statistical precision from 5 runs per configuration, possible judge bias from GPT-5-mini, and evaluation on a single machine only.
sections.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.headline: Frontier models are used only at search time; stated limits include 5 runs per configuration, possible GPT-5-mini judge bias and single-machine evaluation.

sections.body: The appendix describes the five primitives in implementation terms: a model catalog, hardware support, discrete and continuous Agents, and built-in Tools, Connectors and Channels. A TOML spec format and an event bus connect them. It gives the privacy design: ordinary inference runs on-device, while cloud-teacher search sends only eligible scrubbed traces, after a scrubbing pipeline and user trace-eligibility controls. Further sections give the phases of LLM-guided spec search with example edits, descriptions of the 8 benchmarks with 508 tasks in total, and broader impacts covering energy, surveillance risk, teacher-API terms of service and dual-use concerns.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers primitive implementation details, cloud-teacher privacy controls, search-phase examples, benchmark descriptions and broader impacts.
